blocks.content: Covers Assam's key economic sectors — tea, oil & gas, agriculture, and handloom — with tea and petroleum being historically distinctive, heavily tested pillars of the state economy.

items: Assam is one of the largest tea-producing regions in the world, and Assam tea (known for its malty, full-bodied character, produced from the Camellia sinensis var. assamica plant) is a distinct, globally recognized variety.

Commercial tea cultivation began in the 1830s following the identification of indigenous tea plants in Assam (associated with Robert Bruce and further developed by his brother Charles Alexander Bruce); the Assam Company, established in 1839, was the first company to commercially cultivate and market Assam tea.
Assam (Orthodox) Tea has been granted a Geographical Indication (GI) tag, protecting its distinct regional identity in the market.
Major tea-growing districts include Dibrugarh, Jorhat, Sivasagar, Golaghat, and Tinsukia (collectively part of Upper Assam), along with parts of the Barak Valley.

Assam is historically significant in India's petroleum industry — Digboi, in Upper Assam, is home to Asia's first oil well/refinery (dating to the late 19th century) and remains an important historical and operational site.

Major oil and gas fields/installations in Assam are operated by entities such as Oil India Limited (OIL, headquartered in Duliajan, Assam) and ONGC; refineries in the state include those at Digboi, Guwahati, Bongaigaon, and Numaligarh.
The oil and gas sector, alongside tea, has historically been one of the two most economically significant traditional industries of Assam.

Rice is the principal food crop of Assam, cultivated extensively across the fertile Brahmaputra and Barak valleys, with the state recognizing distinct cropping seasons (Sali/Sali paddy being the main winter rice crop).

Other significant crops include jute, sugarcane, and a range of horticultural products; Assam is also known for specific regional agricultural products that have received GI tags (e.g., certain varieties of rice, and products like Assam's Bodo dhan or Joha rice in various contexts).

Sericulture — Assam is particularly notable for producing Muga silk, a golden-hued silk variety unique to the region, which has also received a Geographical Indication tag; Assam additionally produces Eri and Pat silk varieties.
Assam has one of the highest concentrations of handloom weavers in India, with weaving being both an economic activity and a deeply embedded cultural practice across many Assamese households.

The Gamosa (or Gamocha) — a traditional handwoven cotton cloth with red woven motifs on a white/cream background — is a distinctive cultural and economic product, used ceremonially and as a symbol of Assamese identity and hospitality.
Sualkuchi, a town near Guwahati, is renowned as a major centre of silk weaving, particularly associated with Muga silk production.

cells:
Exam Tip

• Muga silk's uniqueness to Assam and its GI-tag status is a very frequently tested fact — remember it specifically as a golden-hued silk distinct from ordinary mulberry silk.

• Digboi's status as the site of Asia's first oil well/refinery is a consistently repeated historical-cum-economic fact.

• The Assam Company (1839) as the pioneering commercial tea enterprise is a frequently tested exact-date/fact question.
